1.s: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar warned against the “grammar of anarchy” in his closing speech delivered on:
1.x: Ambedkar used the expression “grammar of anarchy” in his closing speech on 25 November 1949.
1.tq: Discriminate between closely related Constitution-making dates.
1.sec: Remarks by framers and Constitution Day

1.s: Who stated that constitutional morality “is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated”?
1.x: The statement was made by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar on 4 November 1948. The expression was borrowed from George Grote.
1.tq: Match a distinctive quotation with its speaker.
1.sec: Remarks by framers and Constitution Day

1.s: The expression “Drifting Committee”, referring to the alleged slowness of the Drafting Committee, was used by:
1.x: Naziruddin Ahmed criticised the pace of the Drafting Committee by calling it a “Drifting Committee”.
1.tq: Use the quotation-speaker association as the identifying clue.

1.s: Who described the Constituent Assembly as “a one-party body in an essentially one-party country”?
1.x: Granville Austin described the Assembly in these terms, highlighting its Congress dominance.
1.tq: Identify the critic associated with a political characterisation.
1.sec: Criticisms of the Assembly - representativeness, composition, time taken

1.s:
Consider the following statements about criticisms of the Constituent Assembly:
1. It was criticised for not being based on adult franchise.
2. It was criticised as not sovereign because it originated from British proposals.
3. It was criticised for taking about three years to complete its work.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
1.x: All three statements are correct. The Assembly lacked a direct adult-franchise basis, originated under British proposals, and took about three years.
1.tq: Combine institutional criticism, origin and time-related statements.
1.sec: Criticisms of the Assembly - representativeness, composition, time taken

1.s: The Constituent Assembly took approximately how long to frame the Constitution, as compared with about four months taken by the United States?
1.x: The Assembly took about three years, whereas the United States is stated to have taken about four months.
1.tq: Use the comparative time figure rather than an isolated duration.
1.sec: Criticisms of the Assembly - representativeness, composition, time taken

1.s: Who described the Constituent Assembly as “a body of Hindus”?
1.x: Viscount Simon used the phrase “a body of Hindus” while criticising the composition of the Assembly.
1.tq: Discriminate between similar criticisms by their speakers.
1.sec: Criticisms of the Assembly - representativeness, composition, time taken

1.s: The Constituent Assembly was criticised for representing “only one major community” by:
1.x: Winston Churchill made the criticism that the Assembly represented “only one major community”.
1.tq: Match the exact wording of a criticism with its author.
1.sec: Criticisms of the Assembly - representativeness, composition, time taken

1.s: Which of the following was NOT a criticism directed against the Constituent Assembly?
o: It was a British-created body and therefore not sovereign.
It was dominated by lawyers and politicians.
It was based on universal adult franchise.
1.x: The Assembly was criticised precisely because it was not based on adult franchise. The other three were recognised criticisms.
1.tq: Find the option that reverses a known criticism.
1.sec: Criticisms of the Assembly - representativeness, composition, time taken

1.s: Which of the following correctly describes India's status on 15 August 1947?
o: A sovereign republic with no constitutional link to the Crown
A federation of independent princely states
A Dominion with the British monarch as nominal head
A colony governed directly by the British Parliament
1.x: India became a Dominion on 15 August 1947, with the British monarch as its nominal head.
1.tq: Separate Dominion status from republican status.
1.sec: British Crown's residual role - Governor-General, dominion status

1.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Governor-General after independence:
1. The same Governor-General could, in principle, be appointed for both Dominions.
2. Each Dominion could have its own Governor-General.
3. The Governor-General was to act on the advice of the Dominion ministers.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
1.x: All three statements are correct. The arrangement permitted one common Governor-General or separate Governors-General, who were to act on ministerial advice.
1.tq: Test several linked features of a constitutional office.
1.sec: British Crown's residual role - Governor-General, dominion status

1.s: Who was the last and only Indian Governor-General of India?
1.x: C. Rajagopalachari served as Governor-General from June 1948 to January 1950 and was the last and only Indian to hold the office.
1.tq: Distinguish the first office-holder from the last and only Indian office-holder.
1.sec: British Crown's residual role - Governor-General, dominion status

1.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. India became a Republic
B. Lord Mountbatten became Governor-General of free India
C. C. Rajagopalachari became Governor-General
D. India became a Dominion
1.x: Mountbatten became Governor-General in 1947, India became a Dominion on 15 August 1947, Rajagopalachari assumed office in June 1948, and India became a Republic on 26 January 1950.
1.tq: Fix the first and last events before ordering the middle events.
1.sec: British Crown's residual role - Governor-General, dominion status

1.s: Dominion status of India ended when India became a Republic on:
1.x: India's Dominion status ended on 26 January 1950, when the Constitution came into force and India became a Republic.
1.tq: Distinguish the adoption date from the commencement date.
1.sec: British Crown's residual role - Governor-General, dominion status

1.s: The first law in independent India to receive the assent of the Governor-General was the:
1.x: C. Rajagopalachari assented to the Madras Estates (Abolition) Act on 2 April 1949, making it the first such law.
1.tq: Match the office-holder, law and date without confusing the constitutional statutes.
1.sec: British Crown's residual role - Governor-General, dominion status

1.s: The Mountbatten Plan was announced on:
1.x: The Mountbatten Plan, also known as the 3 June Plan, was announced on 3 June 1947.
1.tq: Use the alternative name of the plan as a date cue.
1.sec: Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) - partition procedure and provinces voting

1.s: Who proposed immediate transfer of power on Dominion status without waiting for a new Constitution?
1.x: V.P. Menon proposed immediate transfer of power on Dominion status rather than waiting for a new Constitution.
1.tq: Identify the person associated with the specific procedural proposal.
1.sec: Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) - partition procedure and provinces voting

1.s:
With reference to the partition procedure under the Mountbatten Plan, consider the following statements:
1. The Punjab and Bengal Assemblies met in separate sections representing Muslim-majority and Hindu-majority districts.
2. A simple majority in either section was sufficient for partition of the province.
3. Both Punjab and Bengal voted for partition.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
1.x: All three statements are correct. The two provincial Assemblies met in separate sections, and a simple majority in either section led to partition; both provinces voted for partition.
1.tq: Test the voting mechanism and its result together.
1.sec: Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) - partition procedure and provinces voting

1.s: Which province decided its future separately under the Mountbatten Plan rather than through the Punjab-Bengal sectional procedure?
1.x: Sindh decided its future separately under the Mountbatten Plan.
1.tq: Separate the individually deciding province from the provinces using sectional voting.
1.sec: Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) - partition procedure and provinces voting

1.s: Which pair of regions was associated with referendums under the Mountbatten Plan?
1.x: Referendums were held in the North-West Frontier Province and Sylhet. NWFP joined Pakistan, while Sylhet, a district of Assam, joined East Pakistan.
1.tq: Start from the sure pair of regions decided by referendum.
1.sec: Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) - partition procedure and provinces voting

1.s: Which statement regarding the referendum in the North-West Frontier Province is correct?
o: It resulted in the province joining India after a Congress-led campaign.
It was replaced by a vote of the Bengal Assembly.
It resulted in the province becoming an independent state.
It was boycotted by the Khudai Khidmatgar movement, but the province joined Pakistan.
1.x: The Khudai Khidmatgar movement boycotted the referendum, but the North-West Frontier Province joined Pakistan.
1.tq: Use the outcome and boycott detail to reject reversed alternatives.
1.sec: Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) - partition procedure and provinces voting

1.s: The Radcliffe Boundary Commission was established primarily to:
o: divide the civil services between India and Pakistan
fix the boundaries between the new Dominions
1.x: The Boundary Commission was appointed to fix the borders between India and Pakistan.
1.tq: Match the commission with its precise function.
1.sec: Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) - partition procedure and provinces voting

1.s: The transfer of power under the Mountbatten Plan was carried out on the basis of the:
1.x: Power was transferred on the basis of the Government of India Act, 1935, while the armed forces were also divided.
1.tq: Distinguish the operative administrative statute from the later independence statute.
1.sec: Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) - partition procedure and provinces voting

1.s: The proposal that provinces could become independent successor states, later rejected by Jawaharlal Nehru as leading to Balkanisation, was known as the:
1.x: The Dickie Bird Plan proposed independent successor states for the provinces and was rejected by Nehru as a plan for Balkanisation.
1.tq: Discriminate between similarly named constitutional and partition plans.
1.sec: Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) - partition procedure and provinces voting

1.s: Which of the following was NOT a provision of the Indian Independence Act, 1947?
o: Lapse of British paramountcy over princely states
Continuation of the office of the Viceroy as the constitutional head of both Dominions
Abolition of the office of the Secretary of State for India
Creation of two Dominions, India and Pakistan
1.x: The Act abolished the office of the Viceroy; each Dominion was to have a Governor-General. The other three were provisions of the Act.
1.tq: Find the option that reverses an abolition provision.
1.sec: Main provisions of the Act - dominions, paramountcy, Constituent Assembly

1.s: Under the Indian Independence Act, 1947, the two Dominions were free to:
o: retain the British veto over all legislation
continue British paramountcy over princely states
1.x: India and Pakistan were created as Dominions from 15 August 1947 and were free to leave the Commonwealth.
1.tq: Test the scope of Dominion freedom against residual Crown powers.
1.sec: Main provisions of the Act - dominions, paramountcy, Constituent Assembly

1.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Constituent Assemblies under the Indian Independence Act, 1947:
1. They were given sovereign power to frame any Constitution.
2. They could repeal any British law, including the Indian Independence Act itself.
3. They were required to retain all British laws permanently.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
1.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Constituent Assemblies had sovereign constitutional authority; they were not required to retain British laws permanently.
1.tq: Spot the absolute reversal in the statement containing “permanently”.
1.sec: Main provisions of the Act - dominions, paramountcy, Constituent Assembly

1.s: Until a new Constitution was framed, each Dominion was governed under the:
o: Government of India Act, 1935, as adapted
Government of India Act, 1919, without alteration
1.x: The interim law for each Dominion was the Government of India Act, 1935, as adapted, until its new Constitution came into force.
1.tq: Identify the interim constitutional framework and its qualification.
1.sec: Main provisions of the Act - dominions, paramountcy, Constituent Assembly

1.s: Which one of the following correctly states the effect of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, on the Crown?
o: The Crown retained a veto over Dominion bills and retained the title Emperor of India.
The Crown became the elected head of both Dominions.
The Crown retained paramountcy over princely states but lost control over civil services.
The Crown lost its veto over Dominion bills and the title Emperor of India was dropped.
1.x: The Act removed the Crown's veto over Dominion bills and dropped the title “Emperor of India”.
1.tq: Pair two related changes to avoid accepting a partly reversed option.
1.sec: Main provisions of the Act - dominions, paramountcy, Constituent Assembly

1.s: Which of the following services-related changes was made by the Indian Independence Act, 1947?
o: Recruitment was transferred exclusively to the Governor-General.
The Constituent Assembly was barred from altering civil-service arrangements.
All civil servants were appointed by the British Crown.
Recruitment by the Secretary of State for India was discontinued.
1.x: The Act discontinued recruitment by the Secretary of State for India.
1.tq: Identify the correct authority-related change rather than a substituted office-holder.
1.sec: Main provisions of the Act - dominions, paramountcy, Constituent Assembly

1.s: The lapse of paramountcy in 1947 meant that:
o: The princely states automatically became part of India.
British suzerainty over the princely states ended.
The princely states were placed under the United Nations.
The British monarch became the constitutional ruler of every princely state.
1.x: Paramountcy lapsed, ending British suzerainty over the princely states. It did not automatically incorporate them into India.
1.tq: Apply the legal consequence of lapse of paramountcy without assuming automatic merger.
1.sec: Princely states - options, Instrument of Accession, Standstill Agreement

1.s: Approximately how many princely states were theoretically free after the lapse of paramountcy?
1.x: About 565 princely states were theoretically free after paramountcy lapsed, although in practice they were expected to join India or Pakistan.
1.tq: Use the stated approximate figure and reject adjacent-number traps.
1.sec: Princely states - options, Instrument of Accession, Standstill Agreement

1.s: Which of the following subjects were ceded to a Dominion by a princely state through an Instrument of Accession?
1.x: An Instrument of Accession transferred defence, external affairs and communications to the concerned Dominion.
1.tq: Recall the standard three-subject grouping in the accession instrument.
1.sec: Princely states - options, Instrument of Accession, Standstill Agreement

1.s: The principal purpose of a Standstill Agreement was to:
o: permit a state to declare permanent neutrality
transfer all sovereign powers of a princely state to India
continue existing administrative arrangements until final terms were settled
abolish communications between a state and the Dominion
1.x: A Standstill Agreement continued existing administrative arrangements with the Dominion until final terms were settled.
1.tq: Distinguish temporary administrative continuity from transfer of sovereignty.
1.sec: Princely states - options, Instrument of Accession, Standstill Agreement

1.s: Which princely state signed a Standstill Agreement in November 1947?
1.x: Hyderabad signed a Standstill Agreement in November 1947.
1.tq: Match the state with the specific agreement and time reference.
1.sec: Princely states - options, Instrument of Accession, Standstill Agreement

1.s: Kashmir acceded to India on:
1.x: Kashmir acceded to India on 26 October 1947 after the tribal invasion.
1.tq: Separate the accession date from the later ceasefire date.
1.sec: Princely states - options, Instrument of Accession, Standstill Agreement

1.s: The UN-arranged ceasefire relating to Kashmir came into effect on:
1.x: The UN-arranged ceasefire came into effect on 1 January 1949, after Kashmir's accession on 26 October 1947.
1.tq: Discriminate between the accession event and the subsequent ceasefire.
1.sec: Princely states - options, Instrument of Accession, Standstill Agreement

1.s: After the Indian Independence Act, 1947, the Constituent Assembly performed which of the following functions?
o: It functioned only as the provincial legislature of the newly formed Union
It functioned as the legislature of British India under the control of the Viceroy
It functioned only as the constitution-making body until 26 January 1950
It functioned both as a sovereign constitution-making body and as the Dominion legislature
1.x: The Act made the Constituent Assembly fully sovereign in its constitution-making role and also made it the Dominion legislature. The Central Legislative Assembly consequently ceased to function.
1.tq: Distinguish the Assembly’s dual constitutional and legislative roles.
1.sec: Constituent Assembly's dual role after the Act  [GROUP-II]

1.s: Who presided over the Constituent Assembly when it functioned as the constitution-making body and who presided over it as the legislature, respectively?
o: G.V. Mavalankar and Dr Rajendra Prasad
Dr B.R. Ambedkar and G.V. Mavalankar
Jawaharlal Nehru and Dr Rajendra Prasad
Dr Rajendra Prasad and G.V. Mavalankar
1.x: Dr Rajendra Prasad chaired the Assembly in its constitution-making capacity, whereas G.V. Mavalankar presided over it when it functioned as the legislature.
1.tq: Separate similar institutional roles by matching each role with its presiding officer.
1.sec: Constituent Assembly's dual role after the Act  [GROUP-II]

1.s: The strength of the Constituent Assembly declined from 389 to 299 primarily because
o: the nominated members resigned before the commencement of the Constitution
members representing the areas that became part of Pakistan withdrew from the Assembly
the British Government dissolved the provincial representation
the princely states refused to send their representatives
1.x: The representatives from the territories that went to Pakistan withdrew from the Constituent Assembly, reducing its strength from 389 to 299.
1.tq: Identify the direct cause of an institutional numerical change.
1.sec: Constituent Assembly's dual role after the Act  [GROUP-II]

1.s: The Constituent Assembly continued after 26 January 1950 as the
1.x: After the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, the Constituent Assembly functioned as the Provisional Parliament until the first general elections held in 1951–52.
1.tq: Use the constitutional transition sequence to identify the successor institution.
1.sec: Constituent Assembly's dual role after the Act  [GROUP-II]

1.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Radcliffe Boundary Commissions:
1. Separate Boundary Commissions were constituted for Punjab and Bengal.
2. Both the Commissions were chaired by Sir Cyril Radcliffe.
3. Sir Cyril Radcliffe was an Indian civil servant with long experience of provincial administration in India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
1.x: Separate Commissions were formed for Punjab and Bengal, and both were chaired by Sir Cyril Radcliffe. Radcliffe was a British lawyer with little knowledge of India, so statement 3 is false.
1.tq: Find the wrong biographical description while retaining the correct commission facts.
1.sec: Radcliffe Boundary Commissions - provinces and chairman  [GROUP-II]

1.s: Sir Cyril Radcliffe, who chaired both the Punjab and Bengal Boundary Commissions, was primarily a
o: member of the Indian Civil Service
1.x: Sir Cyril Radcliffe was a British lawyer who had little knowledge of India when he was appointed to chair both Boundary Commissions.
1.tq: Test the person’s professional identity rather than the office held.
1.sec: Radcliffe Boundary Commissions - provinces and chairman  [GROUP-II]

1.s: The Radcliffe Boundary Commission award was ready on 12 August 1947 but was published on
1.x: The award was ready on 12 August 1947 but was published on 17 August 1947. The delayed publication was intended to avoid Britain being blamed for the violence associated with partition.
1.tq: Distinguish the date on which a decision was ready from the date on which it was published.
1.sec: Radcliffe Boundary Commissions - provinces and chairman  [GROUP-II]

1.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the work period of the Constituent Assembly?
o: 3 years, 1 month and 18 days; 12 sessions and 175 sitting days
2 years, 9 months and 18 days; 10 sessions and 160 sitting days
2 years, 11 months and 18 days; 11 sessions and 165 sitting days
2 years, 11 months and 8 days; 11 sessions and 150 sitting days
1.x: The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days, held 11 sessions and sat for 165 days.
1.tq: Match a cluster of closely related duration and session figures.
1.sec: Time taken - years, sessions, sitting days  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

1.s: For how many days was the Draft Constitution considered by the Constituent Assembly?
1.x: The Draft Constitution was considered for 114 days. The figure of 141 days refers to the sittings of the Drafting Committee, not to the Assembly’s consideration of the Draft.
1.tq: Separate two nearby numerical figures belonging to different stages of constitution-making.
1.sec: Time taken - years, sessions, sitting days  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

1.s: The Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly sat for how many days?
1.x: The Drafting Committee sat for 141 days. This is distinct from the 114 days during which the Draft Constitution was considered by the Assembly.
1.tq: Use institutional attribution to distinguish similar duration figures.
1.sec: Time taken - years, sessions, sitting days  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

1.s:
Consider the following statements about the preparation of the Indian Constitution:
1. The framers consulted the constitutions of about 60 countries.
2. Approximately Rs 64 lakh was spent on the constitution-making process.
3. The Draft Constitution initially contained 395 Articles.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
1.x: The framers consulted the constitutions of about 60 countries and the expenditure was about Rs 64 lakh. The Draft contained 315 Articles; 395 Articles belonged to the adopted text, so statement 3 is false.
1.tq: Use the wrong-stage numerical trap involving the Draft and the adopted Constitution.
1.sec: Time taken - years, sessions, sitting days  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

1.s: Which of the following correctly compares the Draft Constitution with the adopted Constitution?
o: The Draft had 395 Articles, whereas the adopted text had 315 Articles.
The Draft had 315 Articles and the adopted text had 470 Articles.
The Draft had 315 Articles, whereas the adopted text had 395 Articles.
Both the Draft and the adopted text had 395 Articles.
1.x: The Draft Constitution contained 315 Articles. The Constitution as adopted contained 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules.
1.tq: Compare figures belonging to successive versions instead of treating them as interchangeable.
1.sec: Time taken - years, sessions, sitting days  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

1.s: The Linguistic Provinces Commission was appointed by the Constituent Assembly on
1.x: The Linguistic Provinces Commission, also known as the Dhar or Dar Commission, was appointed by the Constituent Assembly on 17 June 1948.
1.tq: Distinguish the appointment date from the later Draft and JVP dates.
1.sec: Linguistic Provinces Commission (Dar) and JVP Committee  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

1.s: Which one of the following was NOT a member of the Linguistic Provinces Commission appointed in 1948?
1.x: The Commission consisted of S.K. Dhar, Dr Pannalal and Jagat Narayan Lal. Pattabhi Sitaramayya was a member of the later JVP Committee.
1.tq: Find the person belonging to the neighbouring committee rather than the named body.
1.sec: Linguistic Provinces Commission (Dar) and JVP Committee  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

1.s: The Linguistic Provinces Commission rejected linguistic reorganisation and instead gave importance to
o: administrative convenience, economic viability, geography and national unity
religious majority, princely privileges, military necessity and language purity
population alone, historical boundaries, caste composition and trade routes
provincial autonomy, separate electorates, cultural uniformity and judicial independence
1.x: The Commission rejected linguistic reorganisation as the basis and favoured administrative convenience, economic viability, geographical considerations and national unity.
1.tq: Select the complete set of criteria associated with the Commission’s recommendation.
1.sec: Linguistic Provinces Commission (Dar) and JVP Committee  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

1.s: The JVP Committee was constituted in December 1948 by the
1.x: The JVP Committee was constituted by the Congress in December 1948. Its members were Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
1.tq: Apply the ‘who constituted the body?’ test to distinguish two related committees.
1.sec: Linguistic Provinces Commission (Dar) and JVP Committee  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

1.sec: Linguistic Provinces Commission (Dar) and JVP Committee  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

1.s: The report of the JVP Committee, submitted in April 1949,
o: rejected linguistic reorganisation for the time being but left room for Andhra if there was strong public demand
immediately recommended the creation of all linguistic States
recommended that Andhra be merged permanently with Tamil Nadu
accepted only the reorganisation of Punjab and Bengal

1.tq: Identify the qualified recommendation rather than an absolute acceptance or rejection.

1.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Andhra in the Draft Constitution:
1. Andhra was included in the First Schedule of the Draft.
2. Andhra was dropped from the Draft published on 21 February 1948.
3. The deletion followed objections from Tamil and Kannada areas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
1.x: All three statements are correct. Andhra was initially in the First Schedule of the Draft, but it was omitted from the Draft published on 21 February 1948 after Tamil and Kannada objections.
1.tq: Check the complete sequence of inclusion, deletion, date and cause.

1.s: Jawaharlal Nehru accepted the demand for a separate Andhra on
1.x: Jawaharlal Nehru accepted the Andhra demand on 27 November 1947. The later Andhra State was formed in 1953 after the continuing linguistic-State demand.
1.tq: Distinguish the date of political acceptance from the date of State formation.
1.sec: Universal angles

1.s: Before Indian independence, the Madras Assembly had resolved to divide the Presidency into which four units?
1.x: The Madras Assembly resolved to divide the Presidency into Andhra, Tamil, Karnataka and Kerala four months before independence.
1.tq: Recall the complete four-part geographical list without substituting later State names.
1.sec: Universal angles

1.s: The immediate historical significance of the Indian Independence Act, 1947 was that it
o: ended provincial autonomy and restored direct British rule over India
combined sovereignty with partition and enabled a quick transfer of power under dominion status
abolished the Constituent Assembly and transferred power to the princely States
created a unitary republic with universal adult franchise
1.x: The Act gave sovereignty to India in the context of partition. Congress accepted dominion status to facilitate a quick and peaceful transfer of power and to support a strong Centre.
1.tq: Select the option that combines the Act’s constitutional consequence with its political context.

1.s:
Arrange the following offices in chronological order according to the sequence associated with the transfer of power:
A. Last Viceroy of India
B. First Governor-General of independent India
C. Last Governor-General of India

Select the correct sequence.
1.x: Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy and also the first Governor-General of independent India. C. Rajagopalachari was the last Governor-General, giving the sequence A, B, C.
1.tq: Use the first/last distinction to place overlapping offices in sequence.

1.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Last Viceroy of India — C. Rajagopalachari
Last Governor-General of India — C. Rajagopalachari
First Governor-General of independent India — Lord Mountbatten
Last Viceroy of India — Lord Mountbatten
1.x: C. Rajagopalachari was the last Governor-General, not the last Viceroy. Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy and the first Governor-General of independent India.
1.tq: Find the swapped office-holder in a first/last comparison.

1.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the relationship between the Dhar Commission and the JVP Committee?
o: The Dhar Commission accepted linguistic States, whereas the JVP Committee rejected them.
The Dhar Commission dealt with boundaries, whereas the JVP Committee dealt exclusively with the national anthem.
Both accepted linguistic reorganisation without qualification.
Both rejected linguistic States for the time being, though the JVP Committee left room for Andhra in case of strong public demand.

1.x: The Dhar Commission and the JVP Committee rejected linguistic States at the time, but the Andhra demand continued and resulted in the Andhra State of 1953.
1.tq: Connect an earlier committee recommendation with the later political outcome.

1.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional position of national symbols:
1. Article 51A(a) refers to respect for the National Flag and the National Anthem.
2. Article 51A(a) expressly names the National Song along with the Flag and the Anthem.
3. The 2026 amendment to the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act extended to the National Song statutory protection comparable to that of the Anthem.

1.x: Article 51A(a) names the National Flag and the National Anthem, not the National Song. The 2026 amendment gave the National Song, including Vande Mataram, statutory protection comparable to that of the Anthem.

1.s: The debate surrounding statutory protection for Vande Mataram has been linked with which of the following?
o: The Objective Resolution of 13 December 1946 and Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
The Constituent Assembly’s statement of 24 January 1950 and Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986)
The Radcliffe Award of 17 August 1947 and Minerva Mills (1980)
The JVP Report of April 1949 and S.R. Bommai (1994)
1.x: The debate has been connected with the Constituent Assembly’s statement of 24 January 1950 and the Supreme Court decision in Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986).
1.tq: Match a current constitutional debate with its specific historical and judicial reference points.
1.sec: Universal angles

2.s: Which one of the following Parts of the Constitution contains the Fundamental Rights?
2.x: Fundamental Rights are contained in Part III of the Constitution.
2.tq: Use the exact constitutional Part number rather than relying only on the source country.
2.sec: Rights and principles → source (FRs, DPSPs, Fundamental Duties, suspension of rights in emergency)

2.s: The Directive Principles of State Policy were incorporated in the Indian Constitution under the influence of which country, whose own model had drawn them from Spain?
2.x: The Directive Principles were inspired by Ireland; Ireland had, in turn, taken the idea from Spain.
2.tq: Separate the immediate source from the source that influenced the immediate source.
2.sec: Rights and principles → source (FRs, DPSPs, Fundamental Duties, suspension of rights in emergency)

2.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Fundamental Duties:
1. They were not included in the original Constitution.
2. They were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
3. The eleventh Fundamental Duty was added by the 86th Amendment Act.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
2.x: All three statements are correct. Fundamental Duties were introduced through the 42nd Amendment in 1976, and the eleventh duty was added by the 86th Amendment.
2.tq: Link the original omission with the two later constitutional amendments.
2.sec: Rights and principles → source (FRs, DPSPs, Fundamental Duties, suspension of rights in emergency)

2.s: The ideals of social, economic and political justice in the Preamble were influenced by the Constitution of:
2.x: The ideals of social, economic and political justice in the Preamble were influenced by the USSR.
2.tq: Distinguish the source of justice ideals from the source of liberty, equality and fraternity.
2.sec: Rights and principles → source (FRs, DPSPs, Fundamental Duties, suspension of rights in emergency)

2.s:
Which one of the following combinations is correctly matched?
1. Liberty, equality and fraternity — France
2. Fundamental Duties — USSR
3. Suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency — Weimar Germany
4. Directive Principles — Ireland
2.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. France supplied the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity; the USSR influenced Fundamental Duties; Weimar Germany influenced suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency; and Ireland influenced the Directive Principles.
2.tq: Check each source-feature pair independently before selecting the coded combination.
2.sec: Rights and principles → source (FRs, DPSPs, Fundamental Duties, suspension of rights in emergency)

2.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency — Weimar Germany
2.x: Directive Principles were inspired by Ireland, not Canada. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
2.tq: Find the single source-country swap among otherwise familiar borrowed features.
2.sec: Rights and principles → source (FRs, DPSPs, Fundamental Duties, suspension of rights in emergency)

2.s:
With reference to the Canadian influence on the Indian Constitution, consider the following statements:
1. It includes a federation with a strong Centre.
2. Residuary powers are vested in the Centre.
3. State Governors are appointed by the Centre.
4. The Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
2.x: All four features are associated with the Canadian model: a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Centre, centrally appointed Governors and advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
2.tq: Group several features under one source while checking that no Canadian feature is omitted.
2.sec: Federal features → source (strong centre, Concurrent List, residuary powers, governors)

2.s: Article 143 of the Constitution, relating to the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, reflects the influence of:
2.x: The advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 143 was influenced by the Canadian Constitution.
2.tq: Use the Article number as the anchor and identify its borrowed institutional source.
2.sec: Federal features → source (strong centre, Concurrent List, residuary powers, governors)

2.s:
Which of the following features were influenced by the Constitution of Australia?
1. Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse
2. Joint sitting of the two Houses of Parliament
3. Residuary powers with the Centre
4. Appointment of State Governors by the Centre
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
2.x: Australia influenced freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse and the provision for a joint sitting of both Houses. Residuary powers and centrally appointed Governors reflect Canadian influence.
2.tq: Separate the Australian federal features from the similar-looking Canadian features.
2.sec: Federal features → source (strong centre, Concurrent List, residuary powers, governors)

2.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court — Canada
Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse — Australia
Joint sitting of both Houses — Australia
Residuary powers with the Centre — Australia
2.x: Residuary powers with the Centre were borrowed from Canada, not Australia. The other pairs are correctly matched.
2.tq: Apply the source-country distinction to closely related federal provisions.
2.sec: Federal features → source (strong centre, Concurrent List, residuary powers, governors)

2.s:
Which of the following features were derived from the Government of India Act, 1935?
1. Federal scheme
2. Office of the Governor
3. Public Service Commissions
4. Administrative details
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
2.x: The Government of India Act, 1935 influenced the federal scheme, office of the Governor, Public Service Commissions and extensive administrative details.
2.tq: Recognise the broad institutional cluster inherited from the 1935 Act.
2.sec: Government of India Act 1935 as source - features taken

2.s: The three Lists under the Government of India Act, 1935 became which of the following in the Constitution of India?
o: Union List, Residuary List and Concurrent List
Central List, Provincial List and Local List
Union List, State List and Concurrent List
Federal List, Provincial List and State List
2.x: The Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists of the 1935 Act developed into the Union, State and Concurrent Lists of the Constitution.
2.tq: Map the older statutory terminology to its constitutional successor.
2.sec: Government of India Act 1935 as source - features taken

2.s: The influence of the Government of India Act, 1935 is regarded as an important reason for which characteristic of the Indian Constitution?
o: Its absence of provisions relating to public services
Its bulk and extensive administrative detail
2.x: The 1935 Act contributed extensive administrative provisions, making the Indian Constitution unusually detailed and bulky.
2.tq: Connect the institutional inheritance with its structural consequence.
2.sec: Government of India Act 1935 as source - features taken

2.s: Which of the following is regarded as the single largest source of the provisions of the Indian Constitution?
o: The Constitution of the United States of America
2.x: The Government of India Act, 1935 is regarded as the single largest source, particularly for the federal scheme, Governor's office, judiciary, Public Service Commissions, emergency provisions and administrative details.
2.tq: Distinguish the largest overall institutional source from countries supplying individual concepts.
2.sec: Government of India Act 1935 as source - features taken

2.s:
Which one of the following statements most accurately reflects the standard classification of emergency-related borrowed provisions?
1. The general emergency scheme is associated with the Government of India Act, 1935.
2. Suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency is associated with Weimar Germany.
3. Emergency provisions are exclusively attributed to Weimar Germany in the standard classification.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
2.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The standard classification associates the general emergency scheme with the 1935 Act and suspension of Fundamental Rights with Weimar Germany; it does not exclusively attribute all emergency provisions to Weimar Germany.
2.tq: Resolve a source ambiguity by distinguishing the general emergency scheme from suspension of rights.
2.sec: Government of India Act 1935 as source - features taken

2.s:
Which of the following parliamentary features was influenced by Britain?
1. Rule of Law
2. Legislative procedure
3. Parliamentary privileges
4. Prerogative writs
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
2.x: Britain influenced all four listed features: Rule of Law, legislative procedure, parliamentary privileges and prerogative writs.
2.tq: Treat related parliamentary conventions as a source cluster rather than testing them in isolation.
2.sec: Parliamentary features → source (cabinet, single citizenship, bicameralism, rule of law, Speaker)

2.s: The institution of the Speaker and the conventions governing the Speaker's role in the Indian parliamentary system were influenced by:
2.x: The institution of the Speaker and the role associated with that office were influenced by the British parliamentary system.
2.tq: Match the parliamentary office with the country whose conventions supplied it.
2.sec: Parliamentary features → source (cabinet, single citizenship, bicameralism, rule of law, Speaker)

2.s:
Which of the following statements is correct regarding the British influence on the Indian Constitution?
1. Britain has no written Constitution.
2. India borrowed the parliamentary system and its conventions from Britain.
3. The Indian Constitution merely copied a single codified British constitutional document.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
2.x: Britain has no single written Constitution, yet India borrowed its parliamentary system and conventions from the British model. Statement 3 is therefore incorrect.
2.tq: Use the distinction between an uncodified constitutional system and a codified constitutional text.
2.sec: Parliamentary features → source (cabinet, single citizenship, bicameralism, rule of law, Speaker)

2.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with Britain as its source in the Indian Constitution?
o: Nominal head represented by the President, analogous to the Crown
Residuary powers vested in the Centre
Suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency
Ideals of social, economic and political justice
2.x: The nominal head represented by the President, analogous to the British Crown, reflects British influence. Residuary powers are associated with Canada, suspension of Fundamental Rights with Weimar Germany, and justice ideals with the USSR.
2.tq: Use nearby source-country distractors to identify the one genuinely British feature.
2.sec: Parliamentary features → source (cabinet, single citizenship, bicameralism, rule of law, Speaker)
